title: Temporary Shortage List: Stage 2 report
key_claim: The MAC's recommended general salary threshold for the Temporary Shortage List was calculated on the assumption that the route does not lead to settlement, and the MAC states the threshold would need to be revisited upward if it does, because settled workers remain in the UK later into life when they become more fiscally costly.
frame_summary: The MAC argues that mid-skill immigration access should be narrow, time-limited and conditional on credible domestic workforce plans, and it prices the visa by reference to the migrant's lifetime fiscal position rather than to the occupation's market wage.
verbatim_quote: we also recommended that the general threshold should be set at least as high as the 30th percentile of the UK's full-time annual earnings distribution (£30,900 in 2025), on the assumption that the route does not lead to settlement in future.
verbatim_list: Our initial recommendation assumed the route would not lead to settlement.
However, if the route does provide a pathway to settlement, visa holders would remain in the UK later into life, when they are likely to become more fiscally costly.
Recent data indicates a substantially looser labour market, with 0.4 vacancies per unemployed person in January to March 2026, similar to the start of the 10-year period shown in Figure 1.1.
As a result, even where shortages are recognised, the design of the sponsorship system can act as a binding constraint on access to migrant labour.
notes: Primary anchor for the pricing rule. Occupation-funnel counts (178, 151, 82, 46, 28) read from Table 3.1 and used only inside the SVG figure.

title: Migration data needed urgently for clarification on settlement, citizenship and integration in UK (report: Settlement, Citizenship and Integration)

# Migration data needed urgently for clarification on settlement, citizenship and integration in UK

23 June 2026
key_claim: The Committee supports decoupling work visas from individual sponsors and tying them to sectors in order to reduce labour exploitation risk, with switching workers required to repay sponsorship costs pro rata.
frame_summary: The Lords committee argues that the pathway to settlement, not the headline level of migration, is the underattended question, and that a settlement system extended without an impact assessment and applied retrospectively is unfair and works against integration.
verbatim_quote: The Committee supports the call to reduce risks of labour exploitation by decoupling visas from sponsors and tie them to sectors.
notes: Tier 1 parliamentary source for the sector-tied-visa recommendation.

title: Why do people come to the UK? Work (Immigration system statistics, year ending March 2026)
key_claim: Entry visas for skilled work fell sharply while in-country extension grants on the same routes rose, and only 30% of the work cohort arriving five years earlier had been granted indefinite leave to remain by 2025.
frame_summary: The Home Office statistics show a work migration system whose front door has narrowed while its renewal channel has widened, with most sponsored workers not converting into permanent residence.
verbatim_quote: Skilled Worker extensions also increased over the same period, up 16% to 199,117.
verbatim_list: In the YE (year ending) March 2026, Health and Care Worker extension grants rose by 25% from the YE (year ending) March 2025, reaching 328,232.
Analysis from the Migrant journey: 2025 report shows that, in 2025, 30% of the work cohort that arrived in the UK 5 years earlier had been granted indefinite leave to remain.

At the year ending March 2026, there were 124,837 organisations registered as licensed sponsors for skilled work and 4,909 for temporary work, compared to 28,734 and 3,952, respectively, in 2019 before the introduction of the new Immigration system following the UK's departure from the EU (European Union).
notes: Quantification spine for the extension treadmill and the sponsor-licence base.

title: OECD Employment Outlook 2026: Geographic Disparities in Jobs and Incomes
key_claim: Labour-market adjustment to trade and technology shocks runs through transitions into joblessness and through opportunities for new entrants rather than through incumbent workers moving across sectors.
frame_summary: The OECD argues that worker reallocation does not in practice deliver labour-market adjustment, so where people are and how easily they can move has become the binding determinant of outcomes.
verbatim_quote: adjustment to such changes often occurs through transitions into joblessness and job opportunities for newcomers rather than because affected workers move across sectors, leaving lasting scars for displaced workers.
notes: Used for the immobility framing only; no numerical claim drawn from this source.

title: Zonglin Lyu: Marking Their Own Homework, After the Deadline: Earned Settlement and the Timing of an Impact Assessment
key_claim: Earned settlement materially alters the position of up to 1.6 million people already part-way through published immigration routes, with retrospective application confirmed, roughly 200,000 consultation responses received, and the economic and equality impact assessments still unpublished.
frame_summary: The article argues that the sequencing of the earned settlement decision, with assessments trailing rather than preceding the rules, inverts the order that public law and parliamentary scrutiny require.
verbatim_quote: a policy materially altering the position of up to 1.6 million people
verbatim_list: its retrospective application confirmed, its consultation drawing some 200,000 responses, its assessments unpublished, promised
The Government's response falls due in late August 2026.
notes: Source of the affected-cohort figure (the Minister's own) and the autumn timing.

title: Migration Committee proposes to cut 24 occupations from new shortage list
key_claim: The MAC recommended 28 occupations for an initial 18-month period, down from 52 on the interim list, covering roughly 4,000 visas a year, which the report said would deliver only a small reduction in migration.
frame_summary: Personnel Today reports the shortage list as a narrowing of employer access to sponsorship whose migration effect is small but whose workforce-planning conditions are demanding.
verbatim_quote: The Migration Advisory Committee (MAC) has recommended that 28 occupations should be included on the government's new Temporary Shortage List (TSL) for an initial 18-month period, down from the originally proposed 52.
verbatim_list: It added that the occupations recommended for inclusion currently accounted for about 4,000 visas a year, meaning the proposals would result in only a relatively small reduction in migration if adopted.
Instead, all recommended occupations would be eligible for the list from January 2027 until June 2028, allowing time for sectors to strengthen their workforce plans before the next review.
notes: Trade press corroboration and the main scale-based counter-argument.

title: Earned settlement: retrospective change is wrong but prospective change is even worse
key_claim: The prospective extension of the default settlement period, and the accompanying extension of employer-tied sponsorship, is a larger and more permanent change than the retrospective application, and the fiscal case for it does not hold because the costs it defers accumulate in retirement.
frame_summary: Colin Yeo argues that lengthening tied sponsorship, rather than the retrospective application of new rules, is the decisive harm, because it converts a five-year constraint into a decade or more of dependence on a single employer.
verbatim_quote: The £10 billion is an estimate of lifetime costs that accumulate overwhelmingly in retirement, through state pensions and healthcare, decades from now.
verbatim_list: will have to wait for a default of 15 years
It is a permanent restructuring of the relationship between migrant workers and the state, and it will shape integration outcomes in this country for decades.
notes: Structural anchor. Canonical statement of the tied-sponsorship mechanism and of the fiscal counter-case.
